uncited: Deformation and Dynamic Modeling extends static radiance field representations to handle temporal changes, enabling the reconstruction and rendering of dynamic 3D scenes from video inputs.

It solves the problem of under-constrained geometry in dynamic scenes by introducing time as an explicit input and using deformation fields, scene flow, or canonical space mappings to align temporal observations.

Unlike static NeRF variants, these methods explicitly model motion, distinguishing themselves from siblings like [Relighting and Shading](17925-relighting-and-shading.md) which handle lighting changes, or [View Synthesis and Morphing](17926-view-synthesis-and-morphing.md) which may focus on interpolation without explicit physical motion modeling.
All methods in this family share the core mechanism of canonical space deformation.

A static set of 3D Gaussians $\mathcal{G}_{canon}$ is defined in a canonical coordinate system, storing base parameters: mean $\boldsymbol{\mu}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, rotation $\mathbf{q}_i \in \mathbb{R}^4$ (unit quaternion), scale $\mathbf{s}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3$, opacity $\sigma_i$, and spherical harmonics coefficients $\mathbf{c}_{SH,i}$.
For a given time $t$, a deformation function $D$ predicts offsets $(\delta\boldsymbol{\mu}, \delta\mathbf{q}, \delta\mathbf{s})$ based on the canonical position and time.
where $\otimes$ is quaternion multiplication and normalization prevents drift.
The deformation network $D$ typically takes spatial embeddings of canonical positions and temporal embeddings of time $t$ as input.
Optimization minimizes photometric loss $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{reg}$, updating Gaussian parameters and network weights via SGD.

It constructs second-order Gaussian motion for dynamic primitives, uses learnable temporal support, creates a binary static-dynamic partition to separate primitives into static and dynamic subsets, and enables continuous-time modeling without runtime deformation networks.
Each dynamic Gaussian requires only eight additional temporal scalars for motion modeling.
This can be thought of as space warping or scene flow.

It shoots straight rays into deformed space and bends them into the canonical scene, usually by regressing per-point offsets for points on the straight ray using a coordinate-based MLP that is conditioned on the deformation.
Currently only supports one object in motion.
For each frame $t$, it extracts a query point $x$ in the observation space and infers the blend weight $w(x)$ for point $x$ using a neural blend weight field conditioned by a latent code $\Psi_t$.
It processes in canonical space by inputting appearance code $c_t$ and viewing direction $v$ into the NeRF network, which outputs rendered volume, density, and color.
It uses the neural blend weight field $w_{\text{canonical}}(x')$ network to learn the animation of NeRF in canonical space to gain dynamic rendering.

The transformation is given by $x' = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i(x) T_i x$, where $x'$ is the transformed point in canonical space, $w_i(x)$ is the blend weight, and $T_i$ represents the viewing direction/transformation.
The concept of dynamic neural radiance fields emerged shortly after the introduction of static NeRF.
